Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, funerals/cemeteries are not impossible triggers, but they are weakly anchored unless there was a death in the accident or major bereavement content. Nothing else in the profile suggests grief- or death-related cueing, so this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for a life-threatening accident. The other items center on fear, disorganization of memory, hypervigilance, and damaged self-view, but do not indicate betrayal by authorities, emergency response, or organizational negligence. This appraisal therefore appears insufficiently supported by the trauma context and accompanying items.

vignette: Aroha sat in her therapist's office, her hands folded tightly in her lap, still working through the fragments of a life that had fractured on a rain-slicked stretch of highway. She had been driving home from a late consultation when a delivery truck lost its brakes on the grade ahead, swerving into the center lane. She remembered the sudden glare of headlights, the sickening lurch as a sedan behind her was struck, the way her own car was shoved forward into the crush of metal and shattered glass. When she came to, she was lying across the passenger seat, airbags deflated around her, the rhythmic thumping of her own heart the only steady thing. There had been no clear sequence of events, only a jumbled collage of screeching tires, the smell of burnt rubber, and the violent shudder of the chassis. In the weeks that followed, she found she could not tell the story to anyone, not even herself. The pieces refused to align, and every time she tried to reconstruct what had happened, the fragments would snap back together in a different order, leaving her dizzy and disoriented. Now, months later, the past did not wait for her to be ready. A delivery truck's brakes hissing at a red light would suddenly deposit her back in that intersection, the full memory rising unbidden and complete. She learned to keep her car pulled over until the image of crushed metal faded, her breath catching as if she were still trapped in the crumpled steel. The world had become a place where anything could shift without warning, and she was certain she could not trust herself to navigate it safely anymore. She started scanning every room she entered, positioning her chair with her back pressed firmly against the wall so she could watch the doorway. At night, she woke to the silence of her bedroom and would rise immediately to check the locks, peering through the blinds until her muscles unclenched. The sudden noise of a garbage truck backing up or a door slamming would make her jump, her shoulders hiking to her ears, her pulse hammering against her ribs. She tried to keep her composure, rehearsing calm responses and forcing her voice to remain level, especially at the clinic where she practiced psychiatry. But the effort to control her emotions left her hollow, and the sight of the hospital's emergency entrance, with its steady stream of vehicles, made her stomach turn. She began avoiding the hospital parking lot altogether, routing herself through side streets instead, which meant she had to turn down new referrals. At home, she avoided sleep by reading until her eyes burned or pacing the living room, unable to lie in the dark when her own thoughts felt like they might spiral. She also withdrew from intimate moments, finding the vulnerability of touch too close to the sensation of being trapped. The distance that followed left her most isolated; she stopped seeing friends, convinced that she could no longer trust her own judgment, and that the world was too dangerous to take any risk. Aroha knew how to map a patient's cognitive distortions and trace their behavioral loops, yet she could not apply that same precision to herself. She recognized that her avoidance had calcified into habit, that the detours, the early nights, the rigid seating arrangements, and the emotional tightening were all strategies to keep the past at bay. These habits accumulated over weeks and months, narrowing her days, draining her energy, and leaving her perpetually braced for impact. She had come to believe she was permanently damaged, that her professional certainty had been replaced by a quiet self-doubt that followed her through every clinical chart and every traffic light. What finally brought her to this office was the realization that she could no longer pretend the fragmentation was manageable. She was afraid that if she did not address the way her mind held onto the crash, she would lose the very tools that defined her career and her identity. More than anything, she hoped to reclaim a sense of safety, to stop scanning every corner and wondering if she could ever trust herself to steer through the world again.
